title: The bee

segments.voice: Yesterday, nadi shodhana: one nostril at a time, left and right. Your line was balance. Did anything even out? Today, the breath makes a sound. Day one hundred one.

Think of the sound a parent makes rocking a baby at two in the morning. Not a song, exactly. Just a low hum, mmm, over and over. Or the hum you make without noticing when you're concentrating, or stirring a pot. Humans hum to settle things, and we've been doing it forever. The yoga tradition took that hum and turned it into a breath practice. It named it after an insect you've definitely heard buzzing around a flower.
screen: `A PARENT HUMMING AT 2AM.` → `WE HUM TO SETTLE THINGS.` → `YOGA NAMED IT AFTER A BEE.`

segments.voice: The word is bhramari. It comes from bhramara, a bee, the big dark kind that drones around flowers. Bhramari is the bee breath. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika describes it: breathe in, and then breathe out slowly, making a humming sound like a bee. That's the whole practice. It's one of the simplest in the tradition, and one of the most loved, because you can feel it working in your own head. Here's how. Sit tall. Close your lips gently, teeth slightly apart, jaw loose. Breathe in through the nose. Then, as you breathe out, hum. A steady, low mmm, for as long as the out-breath lasts, without forcing it. Feel where the sound goes. The lips tingle. The face buzzes. The whole skull seems to vibrate, from the inside. Then breathe in again, quietly, and hum again. If you want to go further, there's a traditional way to turn the sound inward. Put your thumbs gently on the little flaps at the front of your ears, and close them. Now the hum is almost all inside, and the room disappears. Some teachers add the fingers over the eyes, too. Keep the pressure light. Notice the connection to the last few days. The hum makes the out-breath longer, naturally, without counting. Longer out. And when the hum ends, there's a still point before the next breath. The week is building on itself. And the easiest instruction in all of yoga: hum.
screen: `BHRAMARA, A BEE.` · `BREATHE IN, HUM OUT.` · `THUMBS ON THE EAR FLAPS.` · `THE HUM MAKES THE OUT-BREATH LONG.` · then, large: `HUM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the bee breath. Sit tall, lips gently closed, jaw loose. Breathe in through the nose. Now hum on the out-breath, low and steady, mmm, until it runs out. Breathe in quietly. Hum again. If you'd like, press the ear flaps closed with your thumbs and hear the hum inside. If you're somewhere you can't make noise, hum silently, and feel the lips tingle anyway. Keep it easy. After a few rounds, let the humming stop, and sit in the quiet it leaves. The bell holds the time.
Bhramari. From bhramara, the bee. Breathing in, and humming out like one.
Your line: hum. Today, when you catch yourself tense, hum one long out-breath. In the car, in the shower, under your breath at your desk. Day one hundred one.

howItsDone: In Hindu yoga practice, bhramari, the humming bee breath, is done by breathing in through the nose and humming on the out-breath, often with the ears closed by the thumbs; it's commonly used before meditation.

what it means: bhramari, the bee breath: in quietly, hum out long, and feel the sound inside your head.
what a scholar hears: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.68 describes it with the sounds of the male and female bee, one for each direction of breath.

notes: HYP 2.68 describes a quick in-breath with the sound of a male bee and a slow out-breath with the sound of a female bee; modern teaching usually hums on the out-breath only. Script teaches the modern version and summarizes the text as 'breathe out slowly, humming like a bee'. Confirm framing.
Closing the ears with the thumbs (and fingers over the eyes: shanmukhi mudra) is a common addition. Confirm.
Bhramara glossed as 'the big dark kind' of bee; confirm.
